title: Tech Massacre: Chip Stocks Plunge in Historic Wall Street Sell-Off
snippet: Wall Street wrapped up one of its worst weeks in modern history as semiconductor giants crashed and the Nasdaq flirted with bear market territory despite strong non-tech fundamentals.
content:
Wall Street just weathered a historic pounding, capping off a brutal week that mirrored some of the worst financial panics in post-World War II history. Driven by a massive rout in semiconductor and artificial intelligence stocks, the S&P 500 slumped every single day this week, with four daily losses exceeding 1%. Such sustained downward momentum has occurred only five other times since 1945, echoing dark periods like the 2008 financial crisis and the aftermath of the 9/11 attacks.

Friday marked the climax of the carnage. The S&P 500 cratered nearly 4%, officially sliding into correction territory after shedding over $2.4 trillion in market value in a single session. Meanwhile, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite sank more than 5%, effectively erasing its gains for the year, while the Nasdaq 100 hovered just shy of a full-blown bear market, defined as a 20% decline from peak levels.

AI Showcase Turns Into a Bloodbath

The severity of the decline caught many investors off guard, given that the week was intended to showcase the strength of the artificial intelligence boom. Even blockbuster announcements failed to stem the bleeding: Nvidia reported doubling revenues in its first earnings release following the departure of CEO Jensen Huang, and Anthropic launched the largest initial public offering in history. Yet both stocks plummeted alongside the broader sector.

Major market leaders took a beating across the board. Heavyweights such as Nvidia, Micron, CoreWeave, Nebius, and Marvell each tumbled more than 20% on the week. Nvidia alone has erased roughly $2.7 trillion in market valuation since its October peak—marking one of the steepest market cap destructions for any individual company in Wall Street history. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index sank 17% this week, putting chipmakers on track for their worst two-month stretch since late 2008.

A Divided Market: Why This Isn't 2008

While the collapse in semiconductor shares rivals the dark days of 2008, market analysts emphasize that today's broader economy tells a very different story. During the height of the Great Recession, panic was widespread across virtually every sector. Today, non-tech equities remain remarkably resilient.

Consumer staples like Walmart and Costco gained ground during Friday's sell-off, and equal-weighted indexes remain relatively flat since late September. Excluding AI and mega-cap tech stocks, the broader market sits only about 5% below its record highs. Financial strategists point out that corporate fundamentals outside of high-flying tech remain healthy, suggesting this sell-off is primarily a valuation reset for overextended tech names rather than a systemic economic breakdown.
